name: Respirator assigned protection factors — federal OSHA and Cal/OSHA, with maximum use concentrations
description: Assigned protection factors (APFs) for each respirator class under federal OSHA (29 CFR 1910.134 Table 1) and Cal/OSHA (8 CCR 5144), and — the derived layer — the maximum use concentration (MUC) each respirator class supports for a given substance, computed as APF × the applicable exposure limit. The regulation itself states the formula ('The MUC can be determined mathematically by multiplying the assigned protection factor... by the required OSHA permissible exposure limit'), but nobody publishes the computed per-substance table, and OSHA and Cal/OSHA limits differ up to 10× for 66 substances — so the same respirator is adequate federally and inadequate in California for the same job. Answers 'what APF does a half mask have', 'what respirator do I need for styrene at 300 ppm', and 'is my respirator sufficient under Cal/OSHA'. Pairs with the existing workplace-exposure-limits asset (1,184 records, two authorities) — the MUC pages are that asset multiplied through this one.
licence: US federal and California regulatory text; facts not copyrightable, sections quoted with citation.

records.conditions: The employer must have evidence provided by the respirator manufacturer that testing of these respirators demonstrates performance at a level of protection of 1,000 or greater to receive an APF of 1,000. This level of performance can best be demonstrated by performing a WPF or SWPF study or equivalent testing. Absent such testing, all other PAPRs and SARs with helmets/hoods are to be treated as loose-fitting facepiece respirators, and receive an APF of 25.
